character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the world's oldest epic in clear modern English that keeps the plainness and force of the original without the scholar's brackets and ellipses. A first pass of the eleven-tablet epic, rendered and refined tablet by tablet.
introduction: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest great story we have — older than Homer by a thousand years and more, written in Akkadian on clay tablets and lost for two thousand years until they were dug out of the ruins of Nineveh in the 1850s. It is the root beneath much of what came after: a flood survived in a boat, a snake that steals the cure for death, a man who will not accept that he must die. There is a reason Lectio builds Gilgamesh fresh rather than reprinting an old translation. The text is a reconstruction, pieced together from broken tablets that scholars are still completing; the first English versions (Smith, Thompson) are public domain but halting and dated, and every readable complete English Gilgamesh — Speiser, Foster, George, Mitchell — is modern and under copyright. So the Lectio Edition is the primary edition here, not a modernization of an older one: a new rendering drawn from the public-domain scholarly record and checked against the Akkadian. Tablet I sets the whole epic in motion. Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, is too strong and gives his people no peace; the gods answer by making him a match — Enkidu, a wild man who lives with the animals until a woman named Shamhat draws him into the human world.

divergences.older: “him who all things knew,” “who saw everything” (Smith, Thompson)
divergences.lectio: “who saw the deep, the country's foundation”
divergences.note: Naqbu means both the cosmic deep — the fresh water under the earth that the epic later sends Gilgamesh down to — and, by extension, the totality of things. The line says he saw both: the literal abyss and the whole of life. ‘All things’ keeps the breadth but loses the depth; Lectio keeps the depth.

divergences.older: “the harlot,” “the temple-harlot” (19th–20th c. translators)
divergences.lectio: “Shamhat, one of the women of the temple”
divergences.note: Shamhat is a name, and her role — a woman of Ishtar's temple — was a recognized sacred office, not the slur ‘harlot’ implies. She is the one who turns Enkidu from a beast into a human being. Lectio names her and states her office plainly.

divergences.locus: Tablet I, after the seven nights
divergences.older: stresses that he was “grown weak,” diminished, when the animals flee him
divergences.lectio: “his mind had widened; now he understood”
divergences.note: When the gazelles bolt from Enkidu, the Akkadian says he had gained ṭēmu — reason, understanding. He loses the wild and gains a mind. The scene is a loss, but it is first of all a birth, and Lectio makes the gain explicit, not just the cost.

divergences.older: stresses being “tamed,” “civilized,” made tractable like an animal broken to use
divergences.lectio: “he ate the bread until he was full ... and he became a man”
divergences.note: Bread and beer are not a taming; they are the last step of a birth begun in Tablet I, where Enkidu's mind first widened. The Akkadian says plainly that he became a man — awīliš īwe, “he turned human.” Lectio keeps it a coming-into-personhood, glad and full and singing, not a domestication.

divergences.phrase: the king's claim to the bride
divergences.older: “the harlot's bed,” “the right of the first night,” often rendered as lurid royal lust
divergences.lectio: “before the bridegroom touches her, the king touches her first ... it has been his by right”
divergences.note: The tablet states the custom flatly, as a decree from the day Gilgamesh's birth-cord was cut, not as a scene of appetite. The horror is in its being lawful, not in its being lewd. Lectio states the right plainly and lets the outrage land where the text puts it — on the law, not on the bed.

divergences.older: Huwawa, in the older Sumerian and Old Babylonian poems
divergences.lectio: “Humbaba, the terror set to guard it”
divergences.note: The guardian's name shifts across the tradition — Huwawa in the oldest tellings, Humbaba in the Standard Babylonian recension this edition follows. Lectio uses Humbaba throughout, the form of the eleven-tablet text it renders, and keeps his three terrors in the old triad: roar a flood, mouth fire, breath death.

divergences.older: “a heart that knows no rest,” a son “afflicted” with restlessness (Thompson and the older versions render it as affliction)
divergences.lectio: “why have you given Gilgamesh a heart that will not rest? You laid this restlessness on him — you yourself”
divergences.note: Ninsun's prayer is also an accusation. The sense of the Akkadian is that Shamash is the one who imposed the sleeplessness driving Gilgamesh, so Shamash is bound to protect what he set in motion. Older translations keep the petition but soften the reproach; Lectio keeps the edge — a mother holding the god responsible — because the theology of the scene depends on it.

divergences.older: Many popular versions place the winds only in the battle of Tablet V and leave them out of Ninsun's prayer entirely
divergences.lectio: Ninsun asks Shamash, in Tablet III, to rouse the thirteen winds against Humbaba — “Let them rise and darken Humbaba's face, so that the weapons of Gilgamesh can reach him”
divergences.note: The Standard Babylonian text reconstructed by George has Ninsun pray here for the winds that are later unleashed in the Cedar Forest: thirteen of them, named, to darken Humbaba's face so that her son's weapons can reach him. Lectio follows that reading, gives the winds by the same names Tablet V uses, and frames them as a request made now and answered later, rather than weather already blowing — the prayer plants what Tablet V harvests.

divergences.older: “a pendant(?),” “an amulet,” “a badge,” “symbols” — translators differ and many add a question mark, because the word and the line are damaged
divergences.lectio: “she laid a token on Enkidu's neck, and she made him her son and the brother of the king”
divergences.note: The exact object Ninsun hangs on Enkidu is uncertain in the broken text. Lectio says only “a token” — it neither names a specific jewel the tablet does not clearly give us nor explains the object inside the sentence. What the scene makes plain is the act: Ninsun takes Enkidu among the dedicated of Gilgamesh and makes him, formally, a son and a brother.

divergences.older: rendered loosely as “after a journey” or smoothed into a single sentence of travel (Smith, Thompson)
divergences.lectio: “At twenty leagues they broke bread. At thirty leagues they stopped for the night.”
divergences.note: The Akkadian repeats the same measured couplet at the head of each leg of the march, a deliberate drumbeat that makes the impossible distances feel ritual and inevitable. Older translations often compressed or varied it; Lectio keeps the repetition exactly, because the repetition is the point.

divergences.older: “seven splendors,” “seven coats of armor,” “seven garments” (various translators)
divergences.lectio: “seven cloaks of terror”
divergences.note: Humbaba's melammū are an aura of divine, terror-spreading radiance — not cloth, not metal. “Armor” makes it ordinary; “splendor” makes it pretty. Lectio keeps both halves: a thing worn (a cloak) and the thing it sheds (terror), so the reader feels the dread the word carries.

divergences.phrase: the falling mountain, the wild light, the storm
divergences.older: treated as straightforward nightmares; the bad omen taken at face value
divergences.lectio: kept terrifying, then turned good by Enkidu, word for word each time
divergences.note: Tablet IV is built on a frame that repeats: a horrifying dream, then a calm reading of it as victory. The horror and the reassurance are both meant to stay, in full, every cycle. Lectio resists the urge to vary or shorten the frame, so the back-and-forth lands the way it was made to.

divergences.phrase: the soundscape of the Cedar Forest
divergences.older: older complete texts had only a few broken lines here; the forest was a place you passed into, barely described, before the fight
divergences.lectio: “the wood rang with the cry of the stork ... the mother monkeys called and the young monkeys squealed ... a band playing, a drum kept up day in and day out, before the face of Humbaba”
divergences.note: A tablet recovered in 2011 and published by Al-Rawi and George (the Suleimaniyah tablet, T.1447) added some twenty lines that turn the forest from a backdrop into a living place — loud with pigeons, turtledoves, storks, francolins, cicadas, and howler monkeys, a din that Humbaba kept around himself the way a king keeps musicians. Lectio brings these securely attested lines into the body of the tablet, because they change what the heroes are about to destroy: not a menacing thicket, but a garden full of life.

divergences.phrase: Humbaba as ogre vs. Humbaba as guardian
divergences.older: popular versions render Humbaba as a pure monster, and the killing as a clean victory
divergences.lectio: the new lines let Humbaba reproach the heroes for laying waste a forest he was set to guard, Enkidu hurries the kill before word reaches Enlil in Nippur, and the great door goes down the Euphrates to Nippur — keeping the unease the text now carries
divergences.note: The Suleimaniyah tablet sharpens an undercurrent already in the text: Humbaba was Enlil's appointed guardian, the forest a god's preserve, and the heroes know it — Enkidu hurries the kill precisely so word will not reach Enlil. Lectio keeps that disquiet rather than smoothing the scene into a simple triumph. The reader is meant to feel that something was both won and broken here.

divergences.older: some retellings drop the curse, or move Enkidu's doom entirely onto the council of the gods in Tablet VII
divergences.lectio: “May the two of you never grow old. And may Enkidu find no one to bury him but his friend Gilgamesh.”
divergences.note: As he dies, Humbaba curses the two friends: they will not grow old, and Enkidu will have no one to bury him but Gilgamesh — and Enkidu's reproach, that Gilgamesh was listening to the curse instead of to him, is in the broken lines. Lectio keeps the curse where the tablet puts it and in the tablet's terms, because the epic later fulfils it exactly: Enkidu, not Gilgamesh, is the one who dies, and it is Gilgamesh who buries him. The seed of that grief is planted here, in the moment of victory.

divergences.phrase: the allallu-bird and its cry kappi
divergences.older: “the bird of many colours,” the broken wing noted but the cry often dropped or paraphrased (Smith, Thompson)
divergences.lectio: “now it sits in the groves and cries kappi, kappi — my wing, my wing”
divergences.note: The bird's cry in the Akkadian is kappi, which means “my wing!” — the broken wing become a sound the creature is doomed to make forever. The pun is the whole point of the image, and older versions that paraphrase it lose it. Lectio keeps the Akkadian cry and gives its meaning in the same breath, so the reader hears the bird mourn the wound.

divergences.phrase: the creature she makes of him (dallālu?)
divergences.older: “a mole,” “a frog,” “a dwarf,” “a cripple” — translators disagree, and the word is uncertain (Thompson; George; Foster differ)
divergences.lectio: “turned him into a stunted thing and stood him in the middle of his own garden, where he cannot climb up and cannot climb down”
divergences.note: The exact animal or shape Ishtar turns Ishullanu into is one of the genuinely disputed words of the tablet — dwarf, frog, and mole have all been argued. Rather than commit to a creature the text does not give us cleanly, Lectio renders the part that is certain: a small, stunted, helpless thing fixed in the middle of the garden it once tended, unable to move up or down. The horror is the helplessness, and that is what survives the doubt.

divergences.phrase: ina kišādi u qarni — between the horns and the nape
divergences.older: softened to “thrust his sword into the neck” of the Bull in many popular summaries
divergences.lectio: “drove the sword in deep between the horns and the nape”
divergences.note: The Akkadian names the exact spot of the killing-stroke: between the base of the horns and the back of the neck — the place a butcher or a matador strikes to drop a great animal in one blow. Flattening it to “the neck” loses the craft in it; the text wants Gilgamesh to kill like a man who knows precisely where the life is. Lectio keeps the anatomy, because the anatomy is the skill.

divergences.locus: Tablet VII, opening — the council of the gods
divergences.older: Many popular versions give the divine council as straight Babylonian narrative, with no flag that the text is missing
divergences.lectio: rendered as Enkidu's dream — Anu, Enlil, Ea, and Shamash in council; Enlil fixing the death on Enkidu; Shamash overruled
divergences.note: The Standard Babylonian opening of Tablet VII is lost — perhaps thirty-five lines broken from the clay. The scene survives only in a fragmentary Hittite paraphrase of an older version, which is where the divine council comes from. Lectio renders it because the rest of the tablet depends on it, but states it as the dream the surviving line introduces, rather than as preserved Akkadian narrative, and keeps it lean — what the Hittite gives us, no more.

divergences.locus: Tablet VII, the curse on the door
divergences.phrase: the cedar door, deaf and witless
divergences.older: “O door of the wood,” addressed as a thing; older renderings often soften the rebuke into lament
divergences.lectio: “Door, you have no ears and no mind. There is no understanding in you.”
divergences.note: Enkidu curses the great door he built for Enlil's temple as if it could hear him — and the bitterness is exactly that it cannot. The Akkadian calls it senseless, witless, without a mind. The horror Enkidu feels is that the deaf wood will stand in the temple long after he is dust, with some later king's name on it. Lectio keeps the door deaf and keeps the edge, and lets Gilgamesh answer only as the tablet does: he hears it, and his tears run down. (This curse, and the curse on the trapper, were unknown to Thompson in 1928 and were recovered later; Lectio follows the fuller Standard Babylonian text.)

divergences.locus: Tablet VII, the curse and the blessing of Shamhat
divergences.older: older versions keep the curse and the blessing, but blur the blessing as a vague reversal
divergences.lectio: the curse and the blessing built as mirror images — gutter for gutter, glory for glory, the blessing given “with as much weight as he had cursed”
divergences.note: Enkidu first wishes Shamhat a gutter's life — the crossroads, the dunghill, the drunkard's fist — then Shamash reminds him that she gave him bread, beer, a robe, and Gilgamesh himself, the whole of the human life he is now grieving to leave. So Enkidu blesses her with the same force he cursed her: kings and nobles to love her, lapis and gold, no man's house before hers, and the wife, the mother of seven, abandoned for her sake — a courtesan's glory, not a housewife's honor. The Akkadian builds the blessing as the exact inversion of the curse, line answering line. Lectio keeps that symmetry and keeps the blessing what the tablet makes it, because the symmetry is the meaning — the man who learned to be human refuses, at the end, to curse the woman who made him one.

divergences.phrase: the wild animals called to mourn
divergences.older: older popular versions often shorten the list of mourners, or keep the people of Uruk and drop the beasts
divergences.lectio: “Let the bear mourn you, and the hyena, the panther and the leopard, the stag and the ibex, the lion and the wild bull, and every creature of the steppe that ran beside you when you were one of them”
divergences.note: Gilgamesh summons the whole world to mourn Enkidu, in a widening circle — first the roads and the forest, then the city and its elders, then the wild animals, the rivers, and the working people. The beasts are not decoration: Enkidu was born among them in Tablet I, raised on their milk, and the litany calls them back to grieve the one of their own who became a man. Lectio keeps the full bestiary the Standard Babylonian text gives, because the animals are where the lament begins and ends.

divergences.phrase: kīma kallati katāmu — he covered him like a bride
divergences.older: “he covered the face of his friend,” the simile of the bride sometimes dropped or smoothed away
divergences.lectio: “he covered his friend's face, the way a man veils the face of a bride”
divergences.note: The Akkadian says Gilgamesh veiled Enkidu's face the way a bride is veiled — a strange, tender, deliberate image that older translations sometimes lose by giving only the act and not the comparison. The veiling of the dead as a bride binds love and marriage to death in a single gesture, and it carries the whole grief of the tablet. Lectio keeps the simile intact, because the strangeness is the meaning.

divergences.phrase: the broken inventory of gifts to the underworld
divergences.older: some retellings reconstruct or paraphrase the full list of grave goods and the netherworld gods as if the text were whole
divergences.lectio: renders the secure part — the table, the honey in carnelian, the butter in lapis, the gifts displayed to Shamash and the powers of the dead — and marks the long inventory as lost, without inventing it
divergences.note: The end of Tablet VIII, where Gilgamesh names gift after gift for god after god of the underworld, is one of the most damaged stretches of the epic; only scraps survive on the clay. Lectio translates what is secure and stops where the tablet stops, marking the gap rather than filling it. Fabricating the inventory would betray the one rule that governs a fragmentary text — translate what is there, and leave the silence where the silence is.

divergences.phrase: ana Enkidu ibrīšu ṣarpiš ibakki — “When I die, shall I not be like Enkidu?”
divergences.older: “For Engidu, his friend, Gilgamish weepeth bitterly” — the early translators give the grief, but the fear of death behind it is often left implicit (Smith, Thompson)
divergences.lectio: “I will die too … and will I not be like Enkidu? Grief has come into my heart. I am afraid of death, and so I roam the open land.”
divergences.note: Tablet IX turns on a single change in Gilgamesh: grief for Enkidu becomes terror for himself. Lectio keeps the Akkadian's question — shall I not be like Enkidu? — because it is the line readers know, and then the plain dread of death that follows it. The fear is the engine of the whole second half of the epic, and Gilgamesh says so in the same breath: he will take the road to Uta-napishti. Lectio brings the fear up into the open, where the text puts it, rather than leaving it under the mourning.

divergences.phrase: Mashu — šadû ša šuma Māšu nabû
divergences.older: “the mountain of Mashu,” the name carried over untranslated; the sense of it left aside
divergences.lectio: “the twin mountain, the mountain called Mashu … its two peaks lean up against the floor of heaven; its roots reach down to the underworld below”
divergences.note: Māšu means “twin” — the mountain is a pair of peaks, one gate for the sun's rising and one for its setting, and it spans the whole cosmos, top in heaven and roots in the land of the dead. Lectio keeps the name and gives its meaning in the same breath, so the reader sees why this, of all mountains, is the door the sun passes through.

divergences.older: “scorpion-men,” “men-scorpions,” the woman sometimes dropped (Smith, Thompson)
divergences.lectio: “the Scorpion-people … a man and his wife … the terror of them was a thing that could kill”
divergences.note: The guardians are a married pair, girtablullû, scorpion below and human above, and it is the woman who reads Gilgamesh rightly — two parts god, one part human, the same proportion Tablet I gave him at his birth. Lectio names them the Scorpion-people, keeps both man and wife, and matches the “two parts god, one part human” to the wording already used of Gilgamesh in Tablet I, so the reader hears the echo.

divergences.older: "Fill your belly with good things; day and night, dance and be merry; let your clothes be fresh, bathe yourself, look on the child who holds your hand, let your wife delight in your embrace" — the famous carpe diem speech, quoted in most popular Gilgamesh as Siduri's words
divergences.lectio: Siduri gives no such speech here; she questions Gilgamesh, warns him the sea has never been crossed by anyone but Shamash, and sends him on to Ur-shanabi the boatman
divergences.note: This is the most misquoted passage in the epic. The beloved "fill your belly, make merry" counsel belongs to the Old Babylonian version (the Sippar tablet), not to the Standard Babylonian recension this edition follows — Sîn-lēqi-unninni cut it. In the eleven-tablet text, Siduri only mistakes Gilgamesh for a killer, hears his grief, and points the way onward. Lectio keeps the SB narrative clean and does not import the OB speech into it. (The carpe-diem lines are the ones Lectio quotes elsewhere as Siduri's counsel, drawn from the older version; Andrew George reads even them less as hedonism than as a man being told to be content with the lot he is given.)

divergences.older: rendered "the things of stone," "the stone images," "the sacred stones," often with a question mark, since what they are is uncertain
divergences.lectio: “He came on Ur-shanabi, and on the Stone Ones … He fell on the Stone Ones and smashed them.” Their role is left for Ur-shanabi to tell: “you have scattered the very ones who carried the boat safe across the Waters of Death”
divergences.note: No one knows for certain what the Stone Ones were — magical images, talismans, perhaps a stone crew immune to the deadly water; scholars have even guessed lodestones. What the text makes plain is their function: they are what let the boat cross the Waters of Death safely, and Gilgamesh, smashing them in a fit of rage, destroys the one thing that would have made his own crossing easy. Lectio does not guess the object or explain it in the narration; the tablet has him simply smash them, and Ur-shanabi's rebuke tells the reader what they were for. That keeps the irony the tablet wants — the rash act of a man who cannot govern his own anger costs him, and the three hundred poles are the price.

divergences.phrase: ul ibašši mimma šanan — "there is nothing at all that lasts"
divergences.older: in some popular editions (Sandars) the "no permanence" and dragonfly speech is printed at the head of Tablet XI
divergences.lectio: kept as the close of Tablet X, where the Standard Babylonian recension places it — the sleeping and the dead alike, the Anunnaki and Mammitum fixing death, the day of death never told
divergences.note: Where Uta-napishti's great speech on death falls depends on which edition you read; prose retellings often move it into Tablet XI. In the line-numbered Standard Babylonian text it ends Tablet X, the answer to Gilgamesh's despair before the flood story begins. Lectio follows the critical line-division and keeps it here. The speech holds death's double face the way the Akkadian does — death is certain and death is unknowable: no one ever sees its face, and the gods who set it for mankind keep the day of it to themselves.

divergences.locus: Tablet XI, the warning through the wall
divergences.phrase: kikkiš kikkiš igār igār — the reed wall
divergences.older: "O reed-hut, reed-hut! O wall, wall!" (Smith and after) — often read as Ea simply addressing Uta-napishti, the trick of the oath left unexplained
divergences.lectio: “And Ea, the clever one, had sworn the oath with them, but he repeated their words to the reed wall of my house.” Then his cry: “Reed wall, reed wall! Fence, fence!”
divergences.note: Ea has sworn the gods' oath of silence with the rest, so he cannot warn a man outright. He gets around it by speaking to the reed wall of the house while Uta-napishti listens on the other side — a loophole, not an accident of address. Older translations keep the strange apostrophe but lose the cunning behind it. Lectio keeps the oath and the cry to the reeds side by side, as the tablet does, and lets Ea's speech show the trick rather than explaining it in the narration: Ea kept his word to the gods and saved the man anyway.

divergences.locus: Tablet XI, the mountain of the landing
divergences.older: "the mountain of Nizir," "Mount Niṣir" (George Smith 1876; Thompson and most older translators)
divergences.lectio: "the mountain called Nimush"
divergences.note: The name George Smith first read as Nizir, and that stood for a century, is now read Nimush from the cuneiform — a question of how one sign is voiced, not a different place. Lectio uses Nimush, the reading of the Standard Babylonian text it follows, while naming Nizir here so a reader who knows the old, famous form can see it is the same peak. The grounding is told in the same day-by-day drumbeat the epic uses for its great waits — the march to the cedars, the twelve hours of darkness under Mashu — because the holding of the boat is one more of those ritual counts.

divergences.locus: Tablet XI vs. the Old Babylonian — the carpe-diem speech
divergences.phrase: "Fill your belly; be merry; let your wife delight in your embrace"
divergences.older: Many popular Gilgamesh books place the famous "fill your belly, make merry" counsel somewhere in this last tablet, as the wisdom Gilgamesh carries home
divergences.lectio: Standard Babylonian Tablet XI has no such speech; it is not imported here. The tablet's own answer to death is the wall of Uruk — the city that outlasts the man
divergences.note: The beloved carpe-diem lines belong to the Old Babylonian version (the Sippar tablet), spoken by the ale-wife Siduri, and Lectio keeps them where they belong — quoted as her counsel from the older poem, not smuggled into the eleven-tablet text. The Standard Babylonian recension ends on a different and harder note. Gilgamesh comes home with nothing — no plant, no immortality, no secret — and is told, in effect, to look at his city: the fired brick and the foundation of the Seven Sages are the only permanence a man gets. Lectio lets that ending stand, and lets it ring the opening, because the closing of the great walls of Uruk back onto the prologue is the whole architecture of the poem — the one immortality is the work that stands after you.

segments.text: Of the man who saw the deep, the country's foundation, who knew the proper way of all things — let me tell. Gilgamesh saw everything, traveled every road, learned the whole of wisdom. He looked on what was secret and uncovered what was hidden, and he carried home a story older than the Flood. He went a long road, came back worn out but at peace, and cut the whole of his labor into a slab of stone.

Look at the wall of Uruk, how it shines like bronze. Study its foundation; no later king will ever match it. Climb the wall and walk its length, test the brickwork: were these bricks not fired in the kiln? Did the Seven Sages themselves not lay the groundwork? A square mile of city, a square mile of date groves, a square mile of clay pits, and half a square mile for Ishtar's temple — three square miles and a half, and all of it is Uruk. Find the box of cedar, slip the bronze ring that locks it, lift the lid, and take out the tablet of lapis lazuli. Read aloud how Gilgamesh suffered, and all that he came through.

Two parts of him were god and one part was human. The Lady Ninsun bore him, and the great gods shaped his body. He was enormous and perfectly made, beautiful and terrible at once. Over the men of Uruk he towered like a wild bull, and there was no one who could stand against his weapons or his will.

But his strength ran without a rein. Day and night it drove him, and his arrogance only grew. He left no son to his father; he wore the young men out. He left no girl to her mother, no bride to her husband — not the soldier's daughter, not the young man's wife. The people of Uruk muttered in their houses, and at last their cry went up to the gods.

The gods of heaven heard the complaint, and they called to Aruru, the great mother who had first made mankind: “You made Gilgamesh. Now make his equal. Make someone to match the storm in his heart, and let the two of them strive together, so that Uruk can rest.”

Aruru heard, and in her mind she formed the image of the god of the sky. She washed her hands, pinched off a piece of clay, and threw it down in the wild. There, in the empty country, she made Enkidu — a fighter, born in silence, hard as the war-god Ninurta himself. Hair covered his whole body; the hair of his head was long as a woman's and thick as a field of grain. He knew nothing of people, nothing of settled land. He wore the skins of animals. He grazed on grass with the gazelles, he crowded with the wild beasts at the watering place, and his heart was glad in the water with them.

A trapper, a man who set snares, met him face to face at the watering place — once, and again, and a third time. When the trapper saw him his face went stiff with fear. He drove his own animals home, shaken and sick at heart, his face drawn like a man's who has come a long, hard road. For Enkidu filled in the pits the trapper dug, and tore out the traps he set, and pulled the wild beasts free of his hands, so that the trapper could no longer hunt.

He went to his father and said: “Father, a man has come down from the hills, the strongest in the land. His strength is like a rock fallen from the sky. He ranges the hills with the beasts and feeds with them, and he keeps crossing my ground, and I am afraid of him. He fills in my pits and pulls up my traps; he takes the game out of my hands.” His father answered: “Go to Uruk, to Gilgamesh, and tell him this. Then ask him for Shamhat, one of the women of the temple, and bring her back with you. When the animals come down to the water, let her take off her clothes and show him her body. He will go to her — and after that the beasts that grew up with him in the wild will turn away from him.”
So the trapper went to Uruk, and stood before Gilgamesh, and said the same words. And Gilgamesh said: “Go, trapper. Take Shamhat with you.”

They set out together, and on the third day they came to the watering place, and there they sat down to wait. One day they waited, and a second. Then the wild beasts came down to drink, and Enkidu was among them — the man born in the hills, who ate grass with the gazelles, who drank with the beasts and was happy in the water. Shamhat saw him: the wild man, the savage out of the deep country.

“There he is,” the trapper said. “Open yourself, Shamhat. Don't hold back. When he comes to you, take him in and show him your art. The animals that grew up with him will turn from him, once his body has lain against yours.” Shamhat loosened her clothing and opened herself, and he came to her, and she did not hold back. She showed him her art, and his desire lay on her for six days and seven nights, and Enkidu stayed with her until he had had his fill.

When he was satisfied he turned back to his animals. But the gazelles saw him and ran, and the wild beasts of the open country bolted from his body. Enkidu started after them and his legs would not carry him; his knees gave out, the wild thing had gone out of him. And yet his mind had widened; now he understood. He came back and sat down at the woman's feet, and he watched her face and listened. And Shamhat said to him: “You are handsome, Enkidu. You are like a god. Why should you run with the animals across the empty land? Come, let me take you to Uruk, to the holy temple where Anu and Ishtar are served, where Gilgamesh rules the people and lords it over them like a wild bull.”

Enkidu listened, and the words pleased him, for his heart wanted a friend, someone who would understand him. “Take me to the city,” he said. “I will go to Gilgamesh, the mighty one. I will challenge him to his face and cry out in Uruk, ‘I am the strongest here!’ I will change the way things have always been — the one born in the wild has power, and I will show it.” “Then come,” said Shamhat, “and let him see your face. I know where he is; I will show you Gilgamesh. Look hard at him, Enkidu: he is full of life and strength. The sun-god Shamash loves him, and Anu and Enlil and Ea have made his mind deep and wide. Even before you came down from the hills, he saw you coming in his dreams.”

For Gilgamesh had gotten up and gone to his mother to have his dreams read. “Mother,” he said, “in the night I felt strong, and I walked out proud among the young men, and the stars crowded the whole of the sky. Then something like a rock from the sky-god fell down in front of me. I tried to lift it and it was too heavy; I tried to roll it and could not. All of Uruk gathered around it; the people pressed close, and the men kissed its feet. I loved it the way a man loves his wife; I held it close. I leaned my forehead against it, and they helped me, and I lifted it at last and carried it to you — and you made it my equal.”

Ninsun was wise and knew all things, and she said to her son: “The thing like a star from heaven that fell beside you, that you could not lift — that is a strong companion who is coming to you, a friend who rescues his friend. He is the strongest in the land; his force is like a rock from the sky. You loved him the way a man loves his wife, and held him close, and he will never leave you. That is the meaning of your dream.”

“Mother, I dreamed again. In the street of Uruk an axe was lying, and a crowd stood around it. I saw it and was glad; I loved it the way a man loves his wife; I bent and picked it up and set it at my side — and you made it my equal.” And Ninsun answered: “The axe you saw is a man. You will love him as you love a wife, and I will make him your equal. A strong companion is coming, one who saves his friend, the strongest in the land, his strength like a rock from the sky.” And Gilgamesh said: “Then let it fall this way. Let me find a friend to stand beside me.” So Gilgamesh told his dreams.

sections.label: Tablet II
sections.title: Bread, Beer, and the Wrestling at the Gate

segments.text: Shamhat took Enkidu by the hand and led him like a child. She brought him to a camp of shepherds out where the sheepfolds stood, and the shepherds gathered around to look at him. They said to one another: “This man is built like Gilgamesh — shorter, maybe, but heavier in the bone. He was raised in the open country; he was suckled on the milk of wild things.”

They set bread before him and he did not know what it was. All his life he had drawn the milk of wild animals; now they put bread in front of him, and he squinted at it and stared. Enkidu did not know how to eat bread. He had not been taught how to drink beer.

So Shamhat opened her mouth and said to him: “Eat the bread, Enkidu. It is what life is made of. Drink the beer. It is the custom of the land.” Enkidu ate the bread until he was full. He drank the beer — seven jugs of it — and the heart in him lifted, and his face shone, and he sang for the gladness of it.

Then they took water and washed the matted hair from his body, and they rubbed him with oil, and he became a man. They put clothes on him, and he was dressed like a husband. He took up a weapon and went out against the lions, so the shepherds could lie down and sleep. He ran off the wolves; he drove away the lions. He kept watch over the flock in the dark of the night, and the men of the camp lay easy, and Enkidu was their guard — a man awake while everyone else slept.

One day a stranger came along the road, hurrying toward Uruk. Enkidu and Shamhat were sitting there, and Enkidu raised his eyes and saw the man, and called to him. “You there — where are you running in such a hurry? What hard road are you on?”

The man caught his breath and answered: “They have called me to a wedding. That is the custom here — a man chooses a wife and the city comes to feast. I have piled the wedding table high with good things to eat. But before the bridegroom touches her, the king touches her first. For Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk, the bride is opened to him first of all. The gods decreed it; from the day his birth-cord was cut, it has been his by right. He goes in to the bride before the husband does.”

When Enkidu heard the man's words, his face went pale, then dark with anger. “Take me to Uruk,” he said. “Take me to where Gilgamesh is. I will stand in front of him. I will shout in his face, ‘I am the strongest here!’ I will change the way things have always been. The one born in the wild country is the stronger man — and I will prove it.”

He went on ahead, and Shamhat came behind him, and they entered Uruk. The people crowded around him in the street. They gathered at his feet and looked him up and down. “He is built like Gilgamesh,” they said. “The very image of him — shorter, but heavier in the bone. Here is one born in the open country, raised on the milk of wild beasts.” And the men rejoiced: “At last, a man to stand against Gilgamesh. At last, someone has come who is his match.”

That night the bed was laid for the goddess Ishhara; Gilgamesh was coming to lie with the new wife as he always did. But Enkidu stepped into the street and planted himself at the door of the wedding house. He set his foot against the door and would not let Gilgamesh pass.

They came together at the door of the wedding house. They grabbed each other and locked, two great oxen lowering their heads to gore. They smashed the doorpost. They cracked the wall. They wrestled through the street, and the whole of Uruk shook with it — doorframes splitting, the houses trembling on their foundations, the people pressed back against the walls to watch two men try to break each other.

Gilgamesh bent his knee, one foot still planted on the ground — and with that turn his fury broke and ran out of him. He stepped back. And when he had drawn back, Enkidu spoke to him, and the heat went out of both of them. Enkidu said: “Your mother bore one man like you and no other. She is the wild cow of the byre, Ninsun, and she lifted your head higher than any man's. Enlil himself has given you the kingship over the people.”
They threw their arms around each other and kissed. The anger was gone as if it had never been. They took each other by the hand, and from that hour Gilgamesh and Enkidu were one heart.

Time passed, and Enkidu grew heavy and quiet. He sat down and his eyes filled, and his arms hung loose, and the strength in him had no work to do. Gilgamesh saw it and asked him: “My friend, why are your eyes full of tears? Why are your shoulders down, and your heart sick inside you?” And Enkidu answered: “Grief has closed my throat, my friend. My arms have gone slack; my strength has turned to weakness.”

Then Gilgamesh said: “There is a forest far off, the Cedar Forest, and a thing lives in it called Humbaba, the terror set to guard it. Let us go there, the two of us, and cut down the cedar, and kill the guardian. Whatever is evil in the land, let us drive it out. I am set on this. A man does not live forever; only the gods do. Whatever a man does, it is wind in the end. But a name — a name stands. Let us go and cut our names into the world, so that when I am gone the people will say, ‘Gilgamesh did this. He went into the Cedar Forest and he did not turn back.’”

Enkidu had known that forest once, when he ranged the hills with the beasts, and the thought of it stopped his breath. “My friend,” he said, “that country is no place for men. I knew it when I lived among the animals. The forest runs sixty leagues in every direction; who would go down into that? Humbaba — his roar is the floodwater coming, his mouth is fire, and his breath is death itself. He hears the wild cattle stir a half-day off, deep in his trees. Enlil set him there to keep men out, and laid a weakness on whoever goes in. Why do you want this thing? No one comes back from a fight with Humbaba.”

But Gilgamesh would not be turned, and when the elders of Uruk heard what he meant to do they came and stood before him, troubled. “You are young, Gilgamesh,” they said. “Your heart runs ahead of you, and you do not yet know what you are reaching for. We have heard of Humbaba. His roar is a flood. His mouth is fire. His breath is death. Why do you want this? No one stands against him and lives.” But Gilgamesh only laughed, and looked at his friend, and set his face toward the cedar and the long road out of the city.

The elders of Uruk came to Gilgamesh, the great men of the city, and they gave him their counsel for the road. “Gilgamesh,” they said, “do not lean on your own strength alone. Keep your eyes open, and make every blow land where you aim it. The one who goes in front keeps his companion safe. The one who knows the road brings his friend home. Let Enkidu walk ahead of you. He knows the way to the Cedar Forest; he has seen the fight that Humbaba gives. Let him guard your body and bring you back.”
Then they turned to Enkidu and laid the king in his hands. “In our assembly we have given the king into your keeping. When you return, give the king back to us. Bring Gilgamesh home.”

Gilgamesh said to Enkidu: “Come, my friend. Let us go to the Egalmah, to Ninsun, the great queen, my mother. Ninsun is wise; she knows all things. She will set our feet on a sure path.” So the two of them went together to the temple, to Ninsun.

Gilgamesh stood before his mother and said: “Ninsun, hear me. I am setting out on a long road, to the place where Humbaba is. I go to a fight I have never fought, down a road I have never traveled. From the day I leave until I come back, until I reach the Cedar Forest and cut down the evil that Shamash hates — pray for me to Shamash. Speak to him on my behalf.”

Ninsun heard the words of her son, and her face was troubled. She went into her chamber and washed herself with the purity plant. She put on a robe worthy of her body, and over her breast she fastened an ornament worthy of her breast. She wound her sash about her, and set her crown upon her head. Then she climbed the stairs and went up onto the roof of the temple.

On the roof she set a censer before Shamash and laid the incense down. She scattered the fragrant offering, and she raised her arms to the rising sun. Then she spoke to the sun-god, and her prayer was also a complaint.

“Shamash,” she said, “why did you do this to my son? Why have you given Gilgamesh a heart that will not rest? You laid this restlessness on him — you yourself — and now it drives him out the door, down a far road to Humbaba, into a fight he does not know and a country he has never seen. From the day he leaves until the day he comes home, watch over him. When you cross the sky by day, keep your eye on him. When you go down at night, do not let go of him.”

“And when you sink below the world and the dark comes,” she went on, “let Aya, your bride, remind you of him without fear. Hand him to the Watchmen of the Night, to the stars. And in the night let your father Sin keep him as well, so that there is no hour when no god is holding my son.”

“Rouse the great winds against Humbaba,” she prayed — “the south wind and the north, the east wind and the west, the whistling wind, the piercing wind, the blizzard, the evil wind, the wind of Simurru, the demon wind, the ice wind, the storm, the sandstorm — thirteen winds. Let them rise and darken Humbaba's face, so that the weapons of Gilgamesh can reach him.”
When she had finished her prayer, she put out the censer and came down from the roof.

Then Ninsun called Enkidu to her, and she spoke to him before the holy women of the temple, the votaries who served in the house. “Enkidu the strong,” she said, “you did not come out of my body. But here, now, I take you as my own, and I name you among the dedicated of Gilgamesh.” And she laid a token on Enkidu's neck, and she made him her son and the brother of the king.

“Enkidu,” she said, “you are my son now, and Gilgamesh is your brother. Go in front of him on the road. The companion who leads the way must bring his friend back whole. I lay the king on you, as the elders laid him on you. Whatever the Cedar Forest holds, come back to me with my son.”
[Some lines are lost here. When the text resumes, Gilgamesh is leaving instructions for the city while he is away.]

And once more the elders gave their charge, the same words they had spoken at the start: “In our assembly we have given the king into your keeping, Enkidu. When you return, give the king back to us.” So Gilgamesh and Enkidu turned their faces to the Cedar Forest and the long road.
[The rest of Tablet III, perhaps sixty lines, is lost.]

At twenty leagues they broke bread. At thirty leagues they stopped for the night. In a single day they walked what an ordinary man would walk in a month and a half. They were going toward the Cedar Forest, toward Humbaba and the road that no one returns from, and they made nothing of the distance. They dug a well before the setting sun, so that there would be fresh water in it.

Gilgamesh climbed the hill, and he poured out a handful of flour on the ground, and he said: “Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see a good sign.” Enkidu fixed the place where Gilgamesh would sleep, like a man making a shelter against a storm wind. Gilgamesh lay down with his chin on his knees, and sleep came over him, the way sleep falls on all people.

But in the middle of the night his sleep broke off, and he started up and said to his friend: “Enkidu — did you wake me? Why am I awake? Did you call out, or did a god pass by? My flesh is crawling. Enkidu, I had a dream, and it was a hard one. We were standing in a gorge between two mountains, and the mountains came down. The two of us were like little flies in the reed-beds.” And Enkidu said to him: “My friend, your dream is good. The dream is a piece of luck. The mountain you saw is Humbaba. We will take Humbaba, we will throw him down, and his great body will lie out flat on the ground.”

At twenty leagues they broke bread. At thirty leagues they stopped for the night. In a single day they walked what an ordinary man would walk in a month and a half. They dug a well before the setting sun, so that there would be fresh water in it.

Gilgamesh climbed the hill and poured out a handful of flour on the ground, and he said: “Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see a good sign.” Enkidu fixed the place where Gilgamesh would sleep, and Gilgamesh lay down with his chin on his knees, and sleep came over him, the way sleep falls on all people.

But in the middle of the night his sleep broke off, and he started up and said to his friend: “Enkidu, I had a second dream, and it was worse than the first. A mountain stood before me. It threw me down and pinned my feet, and a great light grew brighter and brighter overhead. Then a man stepped out of it — the most handsome man in the land — and he pulled me out from under the mountain. He gave me water to drink, and my heart grew steady, and he set my feet back on the ground.” And Enkidu said: “My friend, your dream is good. The dream is a piece of luck. The mountain is Humbaba. Even if he throws you down, you will not stay down. The one who pulled you free and gave you water — that is the sun-god Shamash, who loves you, and Lugalbanda, your own father, the god who watches over you. The two of them will lift you out of every danger, and we will do a thing the world will remember.”

At twenty leagues they broke bread. At thirty leagues they stopped for the night. In a single day they walked what an ordinary man would walk in a month and a half. They dug a well before the setting sun, so that there would be fresh water in it.

Gilgamesh climbed the hill and poured out a handful of flour on the ground, and he said: “Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see a good sign.” Enkidu fixed the place where Gilgamesh would sleep, and Gilgamesh lay down with his chin on his knees, and sleep came over him, the way sleep falls on all people.

But in the middle of the night his sleep broke off, and he started up and said to his friend: “Enkidu, I had a third dream, and the whole earth was in an uproar. The ground cracked and split. The sky went black as pitch, and lightning struck across it, and fire broke loose. The flames stood up tall — and then death came raining down. The light died out, the fire went out, and everything that had fallen turned to ash.” But Enkidu turned the dream over in his mind and said: “My friend, this dream too is good. We will come down on Humbaba like that storm. Take heart. We will go up against him, and he will not stand.”

And Gilgamesh wept before Shamash, and Shamash heard him out of heaven, and a voice came to him in warning. “Hurry,” the god said. “Stand against him now, before he reaches the deep wood and goes down among the trees and wraps himself in his power. Humbaba wears seven cloaks of terror. He has put on only one; the other six are laid aside. Strike while he wears the one. Once he is armored in all seven, no one alive can come near him.”
[More dreams follow on the road, but the clay is broken, and they cannot be read whole.]

At last they came to the edge of the Cedar Forest, and they stood still. The trees rose up before them, taller than any trees they had ever seen, and the green of them was deep and dark and went on without end.

And there was the gate of the forest, broad and high. Enkidu reached out and put his hand against it — and the moment he touched it his hand went heavy and his arm went numb, and the strength drained out of it for a while. He stood there, his hand hanging useless, afraid; and the tears ran down his face, and he could not lift his arm.

Gilgamesh said to him: “Enkidu, my friend — why are you crying like a coward? You who were never afraid, you who came down out of the hills, who killed lions at the watering place and never flinched — why has your courage gone? Take my hand. We will go on together. Forget death; think of life. A man who walks in front of his friend keeps him safe, and his name lives after him. Two people will not drown — a boat with two ropes does not sink, and a rope braided three ways is not easily cut. You hold me up, and I will hold you, and let whatever comes, come. We have come this far. There is no turning back now.”

So they steeled themselves at the gate of the wood. The strength came back into Enkidu's arm. They looked once more at the dark of the trees and the height of the cedars, and they breathed deep, and they went in.

They stood at the edge of the forest and could not speak. They looked up at the tops of the cedars, where the trees climbed out of sight, and they looked at the dark mouth of the wood where the path ran in. There was a track worn smooth where Humbaba walked, and the road ran straight and the way was good. And there before them was the cedar mountain, the home of the gods, the throne of Irnini. Down the whole face of the mountain the cedars poured their green; their shade was deep and good and full of rest. The thornbushes were knotted together; the undergrowth was a thick mat; the boxwood and the cedar stood close. A ravine ran around the wood, two leagues across, and again two-thirds of that, and there was no easy way in.

And the forest was loud. It was loud all day long. A pigeon was calling and a turtledove answered it; the wood rang with the cry of the stork and rippled with the chatter of the francolin; the cicadas kept up their high singing without rest. High in the branches the mother monkeys called and the young monkeys squealed, and the whole green mountain was a kind of music — a band playing, a drum kept up day in and day out, before the face of Humbaba.

Gilgamesh and Enkidu went in among the trees, and the going was slow, and their courage rose and fell as they walked. They steadied each other on the bad ground. “A slippery path holds no fear for two who hold each other up,” they said to each other. “Two will not be pulled down. A rope of three strands is not easily cut. Even the great lion — two cubs can roll him over.” So they kept on, deeper, until they came to where the guardian was.

And Humbaba saw them, and he mocked them. His voice was not afraid. “So the fool and the half-wit come to give each other advice,” he said. “But you, Gilgamesh — why have you come to me at all? Go on, Enkidu, you son of a fish that never knew its father, you turtle that never sucked its mother's milk — go on and counsel him. I watched you when you were small and running with the beasts, and I did not bother to come down to you then. And now you have brought Gilgamesh up into my forest, and you stand here, an enemy, a stranger.” His face was a horror, and it would not hold still; it shifted and changed as they watched. “Gilgamesh,” he said, “I will cut your throat and your neck. I will feed your flesh to the screaming vulture, to the eagle and the carrion bird.”

Gilgamesh's heart turned over in him, and he said low to his friend: “Enkidu — his face keeps changing. I cannot look at it.” And Enkidu answered him hard, to put the iron back in him: “Why are you whimpering like that, my friend? Why are you hiding behind your own small voice? We have come too far for this. There is nothing left to do but fall on him — strike, and strike harder, and do not lift your foot to run. The smith who would shape the metal blows the bellows again and again until the iron glows. Blow on it. Do not turn your back. Bring down the flood on him; crack the whip.”

So they fell on Humbaba, and the fight was a thing that shook the world. The ground split under the heels of their feet. They wheeled and grappled, and the mountains cracked with it — Sirion split, and Lebanon split. The bright clouds went black overhead, and death came raining down on them like a cold fog. Then Shamash, who loved Gilgamesh, loosed out of heaven the great winds against Humbaba — the south wind and the north, the east wind and the west, the whistling wind, the piercing wind, the blizzard, the evil wind, the wind of Simurru, the demon wind, the ice wind, the storm, the sandstorm — thirteen winds, and they rose up all at once and closed over Humbaba's face. He could not push forward through them; he could not scramble back out behind. The winds held him fast, and he could neither fight nor run. And Gilgamesh's weapon was at his throat.

Then Humbaba, pinned and beaten, begged for his life. “You are young yet, Gilgamesh,” he said. “Your mother bore you, and you are the child of Ninsun, the wild cow of the byre. It was Shamash, the lord of the mountain, who roused you to come up here — this was never your own doing. O Gilgamesh, king, true son of Uruk — let me go, and I will be your servant. I will cut down as many of these trees as you tell me to cut. I will guard the fine timber for you, the wood good enough for your own palace. Only let me live.”

But Enkidu said: “Do not listen to him, my friend.” And Humbaba turned then to Enkidu. “You know the law of my forest,” he said. “You above all — you who lived here among the beasts, you know what Enlil set down. I should have caught you at the gate and killed you the moment you set foot among my branches. I should have fed your flesh to the vulture and the eagle. And now, Enkidu, the mercy is in your hands. Speak to Gilgamesh. Tell him to spare my life.”

Enkidu would not be moved. “My friend,” he said to Gilgamesh, “Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest — finish him. Grind him down, kill him, leave nothing. Do it now, before word of this reaches Enlil where he sits in Nippur, before the great gods hear and turn their anger on us. Enlil is in Nippur; Shamash is in Sippar. Set up a monument that will stand forever, and let it say how Gilgamesh killed Humbaba.”

When Humbaba understood that he would die, he spent his last breath on a curse. He laid it on the two of them where they stood: “May the two of you never grow old. And may Enkidu find no one to bury him but his friend Gilgamesh.” And Enkidu, hearing it, said: “My friend, I have been talking and talking to you, and you have not been listening to me. You have been listening to the curse of Humbaba.” But the thing was already decided. They closed on him, and they cut him open, and they tore out his insides and his tongue, and Humbaba the guardian was dead. And abundance rained down on the mountain.

Then they took up the axes against the cedars. Gilgamesh felled the great trees, and Enkidu went among them clearing the stumps and the brush. And as they worked, Enkidu looked at the tallest cedar of all, the one whose crown scraped the sky, and a thought came to him. “My friend,” he said, “we have brought down the highest cedar there is, the tree whose top touches the heavens. Let us make a door out of it — a door seventy-two cubits high and twenty-four wide and a cubit thick, its frame and both its pivots cut whole from the one tree. Let us carry it to Nippur. The Euphrates itself will carry it down for us, and Nippur will be glad of it.”

So they lashed the great timber into a raft. Enkidu took the steering, and the river took the load, and the cedars went down the Euphrates toward home. And Gilgamesh stood on the raft and held in his hands the head of Humbaba.

sections.label: Tablet VI
sections.title: Ishtar and the Bull of Heaven

segments.text: When the fight was over, Gilgamesh washed the matted hair from his body and cleaned the filth of battle from his gear. He shook his hair down across his back, and he threw off his soiled clothes and put on clean ones, and wrapped a cloak around himself and tied it with a sash. Then he set the crown on his head, and he was beautiful again — a king come home.

And the Lady Ishtar lifted her eyes to the beauty of Gilgamesh, and desire moved in her. “Come to me, Gilgamesh,” she said. “Be my husband. Give me the fruit of your body, and you will be mine and I will be yours. I will harness you a chariot of lapis and gold, with wheels of gold and fittings of amber, and team it with lions and great mules. Come into my house, into the sweet smell of cedar. When you cross my threshold, the doorway and the footstool will kiss your feet. Kings and princes and nobles will kneel to you, and all that the hills and the lowlands grow they will bring to you as tribute. Your goats will drop triplets and your ewes twins; your loaded donkey will outrun the swiftest mule; your horse will run famous before the chariot, and no ox will stand against yours at the yoke.”

But Gilgamesh opened his mouth and answered her: “And what would I have to give you, if I took you for a wife? Oil for your skin, fine clothes for your body, bread fit for a god and beer fit for a king — and what would I get back? You are a brazier that goes cold the moment one needs its fire. A back door that keeps out neither wind nor storm. A palace that caves in on the soldiers inside it. An elephant that throws off its covering. Pitch that blackens the hands that carry it. A waterskin that soaks the man who hauls it. Limestone that crumbles the wall it was set in. A battering ram that turns on its own army. A shoe that bites the foot of the one who wears it. Where is the husband of yours who lasted? Where is the brave man of yours who is not crying?”

“Listen, and I will tell your loves out, one by one. There was Dumuzi, the husband of your girlhood — and you set on him a grief that comes back every year, and he is wept for still. You loved the bright little roller-bird, and then you struck it and broke its wing, and now it sits in the groves and cries kappi, kappi — my wing, my wing. You loved the lion, perfect in his strength — and you dug for him seven pits, and seven more. You loved the war-horse, glorious in the charge — and you gave him for his portion the whip and the spur and the lash; you decreed that he gallop seven leagues without rest, that he churn and drink his own muddied water, and you doomed his mother Silili to weep for him forever.

“You loved the shepherd, the herdsman, the keeper of the flock, who heaped up loaves baked in the ashes for you and butchered a kid for you every single day — and you struck him and turned him into a wolf, and now his own herd-boys drive him off, and his own dogs tear at his haunches. And you loved Ishullanu, your father's gardener, who carried you baskets of dates and made your table shine, day after day. You looked him over and you came to him: ‘Ishullanu, let me taste your strength. Put out your hand and touch my sex.’ And Ishullanu said to you, ‘What do you want with me? My mother bakes; I have eaten; am I to eat the bread of insult and shame instead, and lie under a heap of reeds in the cold?’ So when he refused you, you struck him too, and turned him into a stunted thing and stood him in the middle of his own garden, where he cannot climb up and cannot climb down. And me — would you love me the same way, and bring me to the same end?”

When Ishtar heard this, she went up to heaven in a fury, weeping. She came before Anu her father and Antu her mother, and the tears ran down. “Father,” she said, “Gilgamesh has heaped insult on me. He has stood there and told over every shameful thing I ever did.” But Anu said to her: “And did you not bring it on yourself? Did you not provoke the king, that he should tell over your shameful deeds?”

“Father,” she said, “give me the Bull of Heaven, so I can strike Gilgamesh down in his own house. Give me the Bull — and if you will not, I will smash the doors of the underworld and break them off their hinges. I will let the dead come up to eat the living, and I will make the dead more than the living.” And Anu answered her: “If I give you the Bull of Heaven, there will be seven years of empty husks in Uruk. Have you laid up grain enough for the people, and grown grass enough for the cattle, to last out the seven barren years?” “I have,” she said. “I have heaped up the grain; I have grown the grass. The seven lean years are provided for.” So when he had heard her out, Anu put the Bull's nose-rope into her hands.

Ishtar led the Bull of Heaven down to the earth, down to the land of Uruk. Where it came, the woods dried up and the marshes and the reed-beds went to dust, and it went down to the river and drank the level down by seven cubits. It snorted, and a pit opened in the ground, and a hundred men of Uruk fell in. It snorted again, and a second pit opened, and two hundred men fell in. It snorted a third time, and the pit opened under Enkidu — but he fell only to the waist, and he sprang straight back out and seized the Bull by the horns.

The Bull spat in Enkidu's face, and with its thick tail it flung its dung at him. And Enkidu called to Gilgamesh: “My friend, we two together can bring it down. I will get behind it and take it by the tail and hold it fast. Then you — like a butcher who knows his work — drive your sword in between the base of the horns and the back of the neck.” So Enkidu came round behind the Bull and gripped it by the tail and held on, and Gilgamesh struck like a butcher, sure and unafraid, and drove the sword in deep between the horns and the nape, and the Bull of Heaven went down. They cut out its heart and laid it before Shamash. Then they stepped back and bowed themselves to the ground before the sun-god, and sat down side by side.

Then Ishtar climbed up onto the wall of Uruk, of Uruk the sheepfold, and she stamped and wailed along the rampart: “Grief on Gilgamesh! He has shamed me, and now he has killed the Bull of Heaven!” Enkidu heard her, and he tore the haunch from the Bull and flung it up at her, into her face. “If I could catch you,” he shouted, “I would do the same to you. I would hang its guts on your arms.”

Ishtar called together the women of her temple, the courtesans and the singers and the dancers, and they made their mourning over the haunch of the Bull of Heaven. And Gilgamesh called the smiths and the craftsmen, and they came and marveled at the size of the horns. Each was thirty minas of lapis in the solid; the rim of each was two fingers thick; and the two of them together would hold six measures of oil. He gave them to his god Lugalbanda, to keep oil for the anointing, and he carried them in and hung them in his own bedchamber.

Then they washed their hands in the Euphrates, and took each other by the hand, and rode through the streets of Uruk, and the people of the city crowded out to look at them. And Gilgamesh put a question to the serving-women of the palace: “Who is the most splendid of men? Who is the most glorious of heroes?” And they answered: “Gilgamesh is the most splendid of men. Gilgamesh is the most glorious of heroes.”

There was a feast in the palace, and Gilgamesh made merry. And when the night came on, the men lay down on their beds to sleep. But Enkidu lay down and a dream came to him in the dark — a heavy dream. And he rose to tell the dream, and said to his friend:

When the day broke, Enkidu turned to Gilgamesh. “My friend,” he said, “why are the great gods sitting in council together? I dreamed it in the night. Anu and Enlil and Ea, and Shamash of the bright sky, sat down together to judge. Because the two of us killed Humbaba, and because we struck down the Bull of Heaven, one of us must die. So the gods had decided, and now they were deciding which. Enlil said, ‘Let Enkidu die. Gilgamesh shall not die.’ Then Shamash spoke up for me: ‘Was it not at my word that they killed the Bull of Heaven and killed Humbaba? Shall innocent Enkidu die for that?’ But Enlil turned on him in anger: ‘You went down with them, day after day, as if you were one of their company. That is why you speak for them.’ And the council held, and the doom stood, and then I woke.”

So Enkidu lay down, sick, and the sickness would not lift. He lay in front of Gilgamesh, and his tears ran down like rain, and he said: “My brother, my dear brother — they are letting me go in place of my brother.” And then a strange grief took him, and he turned on a thing that could not answer: the great door he had built with his own hands, the cedar door he had set up in Enlil's temple. He had gone twenty leagues to find the wood. He had searched the forest until he found the one cedar that towered over all the rest, a tree no man had ever matched. He had cut it and shaped it, the leaf of the door and the pivot and the post, all of it perfect — seventy-two cubits high and twenty-four across.

“Door,” he said, “you have no ears and no mind. There is no understanding in you. I searched twenty leagues for your wood, I found the highest cedar in the forest for you — and there is nothing in you to know it. If I had known what you would cost me, I would have raised my axe and split you into kindling, and hung up a gate of woven reeds in your place. Some king who comes after me will hang his name on you. He will take my name off and put his own. And you will stand in the temple, and I will be gone.” Gilgamesh heard what his friend said, and his tears ran down.

Then he cursed the trapper, the man who first found him at the watering place. “Trapper,” he said, “may you never have enough. May your game grow thin and your catch grow small. May the wild things slip out of your nets and your snares stand empty. May whatever you take be the leanest share, and may your hands go home empty before the others'.” So he laid his curse on the trapper, and his heart was not eased.

And then he turned on Shamhat, and cursed her too. “Come, Shamhat,” he said, “and I will set your fate — a fate that will not end as long as the world stands. I will curse you, and the curse will fall hard. You will have no house of your own. You will sit at the crossroads in the dust of the potters' yard. The shadow of the wall will be your shelter, and the dunghill your bed at night. Thorn and bramble will tear your feet. The drunk and the sober alike will strike your face. Because you drew me out of the wild — because of you I am lying here, and the fever is on my back.”

But Shamash heard him out of heaven, and he called down to him: “Enkidu — why do you curse Shamhat? She gave you bread, the food fit for the gods. She gave you beer, the drink fit for a king. She put a fine robe on your body. And she gave you Gilgamesh for a friend and a brother. Now Gilgamesh, your friend and your brother, will lay you on a great bed. He will lay you on a bed of honor and seat your memory at his left hand, and the princes of the earth will kiss your feet. He will set all of Uruk weeping for you. He will turn the whole people to mourning, and the proud men he will bend to your service. And when you are gone, he himself will let his hair grow wild and put on a lion's skin and wander the open country, grieving for you.”

Enkidu heard the words of Shamash, and the anger went out of him. He took back his curse, and in its place he blessed her, with as much weight as he had cursed. “Shamhat,” he said, “let me set your fate again. Let kings and princes and nobles love you. Let the lover comb out his hair for you and loosen his belt for you, and lay you down on a bed of lapis and gold. Let him heap his treasure on you — carnelian and gold and the blue stone out of the storehouse. Let no man's house come before yours. Let the wife, the mother of seven, be left for your sake.”

But the sickness only grew, and that night Enkidu had another dream, and it was the dream of his death. He lay alone, and the weight of it came down on him, and in the morning he told it to his friend. “Gilgamesh, hear the dream I had in the night. The sky cried out, and the earth answered, and I stood between them by myself. And a man came toward me. His face was dark, and his face was like the face of the Anzu bird, and his hands were the claws of a lion. He came at me and overpowered me. He pressed me down. He held me down under him.” [A few lines are lost.]

“He changed my arms,” Enkidu went on, “and made them into wings, into the wings of a bird. And he took me by the wing and led me down — down to the house of darkness, the house of Irkalla. To the house that no one leaves who once goes in. Down the road that runs only one way, that no one walks back up. To the house where the ones who live there sit without light, where the dust is their food and clay is what they eat. They wear feathers like birds, a coat of feathers, and they sit in the dark and never see the day. And on the door and the bolt, the dust lay thick.”

“I went into the house of dust,” he said, “and I saw the crowns brought low. I saw the ones who had worn crowns, who had ruled the land in the old days — they were the ones serving now, setting out the roasted meat for Anu and Enlil, carrying the cold water from the skins. In the house of dust I saw the high priest and his servant, the seer and the man of spells, the priest who anointed the great gods. I saw Etana there, and Sumuqan the god of the herds. And there sat the queen of the dead, Ereshkigal, and bowing before her was Belet-seri, who keeps the records of the underworld, reading the tablet aloud in her presence. She lifted her head, and she looked at me.” [The rest of the dream is lost.]

When Enkidu had told the dream, he could not rise from it. The fever took him in earnest, and he lay on his bed and grew weaker, and the days went by, and he did not get up. He lay there day after day, and the sickness fed on him, and Gilgamesh sat beside him and could do nothing.

And Enkidu lifted his eyes to his friend and said the thing that was hardest of all. “I am not dying the way a man wants to die. The man who falls in battle falls clean — his friends see it, and his name goes on, and people say of him, ‘There was a man.’ But I am dying in a bed. I will waste away and die of sickness, and there is no glory in it, and no name. Gilgamesh — I am dying like this, and not like a man.”
[The last lines of Tablet VII are broken: the days of Enkidu's sickness, and his death.]

As soon as the first light broke, Gilgamesh opened his mouth and made his lament over Enkidu. “Enkidu, my friend — your mother was a gazelle, your father a wild donkey of the steppe, and the wild asses raised you on their milk, and the herds of the open country taught you every pasture and watering place. Now I weep for you, Enkidu, and I cannot stop.”

“Let the roads weep for you — the roads we walked together to the Cedar Forest. Let them mourn you day and night and never fall silent. Let the elders of broad-streeted Uruk mourn you, the ones who stood behind us with their blessing when we set out. Let the high country mourn you, the ridges we climbed side by side. Let the open land cry out for you as if it were your mother.”

“Let the cypress and the cedar mourn you, the great trees we cut our way through in our anger. Let the bear mourn you, and the hyena, the panther and the leopard, the stag and the ibex, the lion and the wild bull, and every creature of the steppe that ran beside you when you were one of them. Let the holy river Ulaya mourn you, the river along whose bank we used to walk in our pride. Let the pure Euphrates mourn you, the water we poured out from our skins. Let the young men of Uruk mourn you, who watched us strike down the Bull of Heaven. Let the plowman mourn you at his furrow, the one who sang your name into his work; let the herdsman who mixed butter and beer for your mouth mourn you; let the brewer who poured you the good beer mourn you; let the woman of the temple, who rubbed your body with sweet oil, mourn you; let everyone who set a wedding feast and saw you mourn you. Let them all weep for you, Enkidu, my brother.”

“Hear me, men of Uruk; hear me, you elders. I weep for Enkidu, my friend. I cry out like a woman who is keening over the dead. He was the axe at my side, the bow in my hand, the dagger at my belt, the shield that went before me. He was my finest robe, the broad sash around my waist. And an evil thing has risen up and stolen him from me.”

“My friend, you ran with me over the hills; together we caught the Bull of Heaven and killed it; together we threw down Humbaba, who lived in the Cedar Forest. What is this sleep that has taken hold of you now? You have gone dark, and you do not hear me.”

But Enkidu did not lift his eyes. Gilgamesh reached for his heart and laid his hand against it, and it was still; there was no beat under his hand. Then he covered his friend's face, the way a man veils the face of a bride. He circled the body again and again, back and forth, like an eagle wheeling overhead — like a lioness whose cubs have been taken from the pit, turning and turning with nowhere to go.
He tore out his hair in fistfuls and let it fall. He ripped off his fine clothes and flung them down on the ground as if they were a filthy thing, a thing he could not bear to touch.

Again, as soon as the first light broke, Gilgamesh cried out across the land. He called to the coppersmith and the goldsmith, the stonecutter and the jeweler. “Make a likeness of my friend. Make a statue of Enkidu.” And he laid out for them what they were to make: the body of gold, the chest of lapis lazuli, the skin laid over with precious stone — a figure such as no craftsman had ever shaped before, so that his friend would be honored and not forgotten.

“I will lay you down on a great bed,” he said to Enkidu. “I will lay you on a bed of honor. I will give you the seat of rest, the seat at my left hand, and the rulers of the earth will kiss your feet. I will make all of Uruk weep for you and turn the whole glad people to mourning, and when you are gone I will let my own hair grow wild, and put on a lion's skin, and walk out into the open country.”

When the next day's light came, Gilgamesh broke the seal on his treasure-house. He brought out a great table cut from precious wood and set it where Shamash, the sun-god, could see it. He filled a bowl of carnelian with honey, and he filled a bowl of lapis lazuli with butter, and he set them out and lifted them up to Shamash.

He brought out his finest things — the rich gear and the worked metal and the bright stone laid up in the treasury — and he displayed them one by one, gifts to be carried down to the powers of the underworld. He set out a gift for the queen of the dead, and for the gods who govern the house of dust, and showed each one to Shamash, so that they would welcome his friend and walk at his side.

[Here the tablet is badly broken. What follows is the heart of the funeral — the long inventory of the grave goods Gilgamesh sends down with Enkidu, named gift by named gift, god by god of the underworld. Parts of it survive: a flask, a throwing-stick of fine wood, vessels of carnelian and lapis, weapons and ornaments, each presented to a named netherworld power. The full list cannot be read.]

What is certain is the shape of it: a king emptying his storehouse for a friend, laying out treasure to buy him a good place among the dead, and weeping all the while. And it is certain how it ends. The offerings are made; the gifts go down; the gods of the dark country are honored; and Gilgamesh, having done everything that can be done for Enkidu, has still not been given back the one thing he wants, which is his friend alive. From this grief he will not recover. When the mourning is finished he does not go home to his bed. He turns his back on Uruk and walks out into the wilderness — and the long road that the rest of the epic follows, the road to the one man who never died, begins here, at the body of Enkidu.
[The close of Tablet VIII, the last of the funeral rites, is lost.]

Gilgamesh wept for Enkidu, his friend, and the bitterness of it drove him out into the wild country. “I will die too,” he said to himself, “and will I not be like Enkidu? Grief has come into my heart. I am afraid of death, and so I roam the open land. I will take the road to Uta-napishti, the son of Ubar-Tutu, and I will go quickly.”

He kept on, out past the edge of the settled world, until he came to the passes of the mountains. There were lions in those passes, and at night he was afraid. He lifted his eyes to the moon-god Sin and prayed: keep me alive. He took up his axe in his hand and drew the sword from his belt, and he fell on the lions the way an arrow falls, and scattered them, and killed them, and made nothing of them. [About two dozen lines are lost.]
And he set his face to the road, however long it was, and went.

He came at last to the twin mountain, the mountain called Mashu. Day after day Mashu keeps the watch over the going-out and the coming-in of the sun. Its two peaks lean up against the floor of heaven; its roots reach down to the underworld below. At its gate the sun comes up in the morning, and into its gate the sun goes down at night. It was the door the sun passed through, and there was no other like it.

The Scorpion-people kept the gate of it — a man and his wife. The terror of them was a thing that could kill; the dread they shed went out over the mountains. When the sun rose and when it set, it was they who watched over it. Gilgamesh saw them, and the fear of it covered his face and went dark over him; but he gathered himself, and bowed his head, and went on toward them.
